summary:
Indiana is a state within the United States, and a visitor to Indiana stands under the national framework on travel documents and entry. Executive Order 14168 of January 2025 redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and directed that federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth.

Passport treatment carries the sharpest document risk. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and now issues passports only as M or F from supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X remain valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and in November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.

Visa screening carries separate exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged under the internal code SWS25 and an application listing a gender other than sex assigned at birth treated as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban. Screening at US checkpoints can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy.

Indiana's own identity-document route closed on 1 February 2026, when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban took effect and ended the long-standing option of changing the gender marker on a driver's licence or state identification card through a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement. LGBTQ advocates who testified against the administrative rule change warned that it would forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents, and the change proceeded despite public pushback.

Facilities restrictions are advancing through the Indiana General Assembly. On 27 January 2026 the Indiana Senate approved Senate Bill 182 by a 37-8 party-line vote and sent it to the House. The bill would require public K-12 schools and state universities to designate multi-person restrooms, locker rooms and changing areas for use only by males or females based on reproductive biology at birth, barring transgender students from facilities matching their gender identity. It would also create legal definitions for sex and gender, bar amendments to birth certificates, and restrict housing in prisons. The sponsor, Senator Liz Brown, a Republican from Fort Wayne, said the proposal lets women continue to have their private spaces; opponents including GenderNexus argued that the provision letting anyone directly or indirectly injured sue a school over an alleged violation would encourage harassment-style enforcement.

Birth-certificate marker changes are unavailable through the courts. In May 2023 the Indiana Supreme Court declined, in split votes, to hear two cases brought by transgender girls seeking to change the gender designation on their birth certificates, leaving standing appellate rulings that trial courts lack authority to grant such changes unless the General Assembly codifies them. One of the cases concerned a nine-year-old transgender girl whose birth certificate's male designation allowed her school to restrict her bathroom access.

A February 2026 national legal risk assessment places Indiana among the harshest anti-trans states in the country, identifying the state's 2026 identification policy and the escalation of bathroom restrictions as the drivers of risk for adults.
tangentialFactors:
Indiana's 2026 identification and facilities measures sit inside a national pattern. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states, while 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at another state's capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.

Document rules are tightening elsewhere under the same national framework. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four.

Federal policy shapes the environment in which Indiana enforces. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, some hospitals paused care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed more than 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.

Custody conditions at federal level document serious harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy, while the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners it holds from 2025. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting radical gender ideology, and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Foreign governments have responded to the national document and data rules. In April 2025 several countries issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States, and in March 2025 at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.
localsOnly:
Indiana residents lost the option to change the gender marker on a driver's licence or state identification card when the Bureau of Motor Vehicles ban took effect on 1 February 2026. The route that had allowed such a change through a court-ordered gender change or a physician statement no longer exists, and the closure came through an administrative rule change the Bureau initiated rather than through legislation.

Birth certificates are a separate and older barrier. The Indiana Supreme Court's May 2023 denials left appellate rulings holding that trial courts cannot grant gender-designation changes on birth certificates unless the General Assembly codifies the authority, so residents seeking such a change need legislative action first.

Senate Bill 182 would add statutory layers to both problems. Beyond the school and university restroom, locker room and changing-area designations, the bill would write legal definitions of sex and gender into state law, prohibit amendments to birth certificates, and restrict housing assignments in prisons. Its private right of action lets anyone directly or indirectly injured sue a school over an alleged facility violation.

Advocates testified that the identification changes will forcibly out transgender and nonbinary residents in everyday encounters where a licence or state ID is requested, and GenderNexus has argued that the school enforcement provision invites harassment-style complaints.
outOfScopeNotes:
Senate Bill 182 had passed the Indiana Senate by a 37-8 vote on 27 January 2026 and moved to the House; its final enactment, any Senate-House differences, and its effective date are unresolved in the available sources.

Whether Indiana criminalises restroom or facility use by transgender people, in schools or elsewhere, is not sourced here. The inventory records the pending designation requirements and the civil suit provision but no criminal penalty attaching to Indiana facility use.

The source inventory does not address Indiana hate-crime statutes, any statewide protection on grounds of gender identity, or how the 2026 identification change is enforced against visitors whose federal passport marker differs from their Indiana licence.

Whether Indiana has adopted a birth-certificate restriction statute comparable to the pending bill, beyond the 2023 court rulings, is unresolved.

The inventory does not record any Indiana arrest, prosecution or reported violence against a trans person under the state's identification or facilities rules, and offers no Indiana-specific figure on asylum, detention or hate-crime incidents.
